open_points.subject: A20 host kernel as a release dependency
open_points.text: A release names every dependency it runs with, at an exact version, with its digest
open_points.question: Does the Linux kernel that runs Registry count as a dependency governed by rule 1, despite rule 6 saying that no kernel version is named?
options: The kernel is a dependency, so its exact version and digest must be fixed; rule 6 must stop saying that no version is named.
The kernel is a host prerequisite outside rule 1; only the base image, Python and Python packages belong to the release dependency list.
The kernel is a dependency but is an explicit exception to rule 1's exact-version-and-digest requirement.
open_points.default_guess: Treat the kernel as a host prerequisite outside the release dependency list and state that exception explicitly.

witness.initial: A release contains the fixed base image, CPython and packages and is installed on Linux kernel 6.12.
events: The release builder applies rule 1 to everything Registry runs with.
The installer applies rule 6, which requires Linux but names no kernel version.
outcomes: The builder refuses the release because kernel 6.12 has no declared exact version and digest.
The builder makes the release because the host kernel is not one of rule 1's release dependencies.
witness.observer: The release operator sees whether the same release is made.

open_points.subject: A20 runtime-loaded code prohibition
open_points.text: A release with a dependency that loads code at run time from outside the release is not made (rule 4).
open_points.question: What counts as “code”, “loads”, and “outside the release” for this refusal—for example native shared libraries supplied by the host, executable helpers, plugins, generated modules, dynamically downloaded modules, or configuration interpreted by a dependency?
options: Forbid only executable modules or libraries obtained after installation from outside the fixed base image and release artifacts.
Forbid every executable file or library not enumerated by digest in the release, including host-provided libraries and helpers.
Forbid network-fetched code and plugins, but permit documented host libraries, subprocess helpers and interpreted configuration.
open_points.default_guess: Forbid importing, loading, executing or downloading executable modules, libraries, plugins or helpers not contained in the digest-fixed release or base image; do not classify ordinary data configuration as code.

witness.initial: A digest-fixed dependency starts Registry and dynamically loads a plugin from a mounted host directory.
events: The release process evaluates required test 6.
One implementer treats the plugin as runtime-loaded external code; another treats the mounted plugin as deployment configuration.
outcomes: The release is made and Registry loads the plugin.
witness.observer: The release operator and the running instance see whether the plugin executes.

open_points.subject: A20 supported Linux semantics
open_points.text: Another system, or a Linux or file system on which a call Registry's rules rely on — opening a file without following a link, binding a listening socket, renaming, flushing — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: Registry neither tests for it nor defines what it does there.
open_points.question: Which documented semantics must a Linux kernel and file system provide for the files_artifacts and concurrency guarantees to apply, given that no Linux version, file-system set, or documentation baseline is named?
options: Support every Linux kernel and file system, conditional on all relied-on calls having the required semantics stated explicitly in A20.
Name a minimum kernel/API baseline and the supported file systems.
Keep an unrestricted Linux version but enumerate the required observable semantics for no-follow opening, exclusive binding, atomic rename and durable flushing.
open_points.default_guess: Enumerate the observable syscall and durability semantics required, without fixing a kernel version or particular file-system implementation.

witness.initial: Registry runs on a Linux kernel over a file system whose rename is atomic but whose flush does not make the renamed directory entry durable after power loss.
events: Registry completes a backup using rename and flush.
The host loses power immediately afterward.
outcomes: The backup guarantee applies because the platform is Linux and the operations completed successfully.
The environment is unsupported because its flush semantics do not satisfy the unstated Linux documentation baseline, so no backup guarantee applies.
witness.observer: The owner sees whether the supposedly kept backup survives restart.

open_points.subject: A21 security-review status after the current A20 change
open_points.question: Has A21 been performed again against the current A20 change, including the external-code refusal and the non-Linux-kernel installation refusal, or must its status remain reopened until that review is recorded?
options: Record a new A21 review of every category naming A20 and then retain PERFORMED.
Mark the review reopened and do not claim PERFORMED until the review occurs.
State that the existing final A20 review already covered the current wording and tests 6–7, and correct its stale description to demonstrate that coverage.
open_points.default_guess: Treat A21 as reopened and record a new review before restoring PERFORMED.

witness.initial: A21 is marked PERFORMED and names A20 under dependencies, files_artifacts and concurrency.
events: A20 is changed after its latest review.
A21 rule 2 says: “A change to a decision a category names reopens this review.”
outcomes: The State 2 security review remains complete and passes.
The review is open and State 2 cannot claim completion until A20's affected categories are reviewed again.
witness.observer: The State 2 gate and later security reviewers see different completion states.

open_points.subject: A21 account of A20's host requirement
open_points.text: Under dependencies, the host and the Python version join the release's list, and test 5 shows them.
open_points.question: Must this passage say that the base image and exact Python release join the release list while the running kernel is a separate installation prerequisite shown by test 7?
options: Replace “host” with “base image”; say test 5 covers the base image and CPython 3.12 constraint and test 7 covers the running kernel.
Add the host kernel to the release list with an exact version and digest so the existing passage becomes true.
Define “host” here to mean only the base image, despite A20 now distinguishing the kernel from the base image.
open_points.default_guess: Replace “host” with “base image” and cite test 7 separately for the kernel.

witness.initial: The release list contains the base-image digest and exact CPython release but no host-kernel entry.
events: The release is installed on a non-Linux kernel.
A21's stated evidence is checked against A20 required tests.
outcomes: Test 5 is treated as proof of the host requirement even though it tests only the base image and Python.
Test 7 is required and the installation fails because the running kernel is not Linux's.
witness.observer: The security reviewer sees whether the host guarantee has actually been shown.

open_points.subject: A20 release dependency verification
open_points.text: These are tests of the release process (rule 5), shown there and not by a check of Registry:
open_points.question: How will the release process establish the complete transitive dependency list, bind each listed item to its digest, compare the installed/running environment with it, and detect a dependency that loads external code?
options: Factory checks inspect lock files, distribution artifacts and the base-image manifest statically; consequence: deterministic admission, but runtime-only loading paths need an additional rule or check.
Factory checks build and execute an instrumented release that records imports, libraries and executed helpers; consequence: runtime evidence is stronger but covers only exercised paths.

Use static factory checks plus a constrained runtime environment that denies access to executable code outside the release; consequence: both declaration and enforcement are covered, with more deployment constraints.
open_points.default_guess: Use static factory checks for the complete locked closure and artifact digests, combined with a runtime boundary that prevents loading or executing code outside the fixed release and base image.
consequences: A static-only choice can miss conditional runtime loading.
A dynamic-only choice can miss unexercised paths and make reproducibility depend on test coverage.
A combined choice requires the factory and runtime boundary to agree on the definition of the release.
open_points.requirement: A release with a dependency that loads code at run time from outside the release is not made (rule 4).

open_points.subject: A20 non-Linux installation enforcement
open_points.text: Installing a release on a host whose kernel is not Linux's fails, and no instance of it starts (rule 6).
open_points.question: Which installation or deployment boundary is responsible for identifying the kernel that actually runs Registry and preventing every Registry process from starting on a non-Linux kernel?
options: The installer checks the target kernel before installing or starting; consequence: direct enforcement, but every installation entry point must use that installer.
The deployment platform schedules the release only into Linux VMs and rejects other targets; consequence: centralized enforcement, but the platform constraint must cover recovery and manual starts.
The release executable performs an early kernel check; consequence: all starts are covered, but the check becomes Registry code despite rule 5 saying Registry's own code reads none of this.
open_points.default_guess: Make the deployment platform or installer enforce the kernel prerequisite before process creation, with recovery and manual-start paths subject to the same gate.
consequences: Installer enforcement fails if an alternate start path bypasses it.
Platform enforcement must identify the kernel of the VM or environment that actually runs Registry, not merely the build image.
Executable self-checking conflicts with the stated ownership boundary unless A20 is changed.
open_points.requirement: Installing a release on a host whose kernel is not Linux's fails, and no instance of it starts (rule 6).
